opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the human collaboration part is the harder part, and it's the part people underrate going in. When you're writing code, the problems are frustrating, but they're legible. The bug is there, you can find it, and the computer isn't going to change its mind about what it wants from you halfway through. You can sit with it long enough and eventually it yields.

With people, especially on a research project where nobody actually knows the answer yet, so much of the work is aligning on what question you're even trying to answer. Everyone comes in with slightly different intuitions about what's interesting, what counts as a result, and what's worth spending the next three weeks on. Those differences are often invisible until they suddenly aren't, and then you realize two people have been optimizing for different things the whole time.

There's also the uncertainty piece. In research, most of your experiments don't work. When you're doing that alone, it's discouraging but manageable. When you're doing it as a team, you have to keep people motivated and keep trust high while results are ambiguous, and you have to be honest about when an idea is dead without making anyone feel like their contribution was wasted. That's a social skill, not a technical one, and nobody really trains you for it in a PhD.

That said, I think the best research really does come out of good collaboration. The ideas I'm proudest of usually came from a conversation where someone pushed back on something I was sure about. So the difficulty is worth it. The code is the part you can get better at with reps; the collaboration is the part you have to keep paying attention to the whole way through.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the human collaboration part is often the harder part, and it took me a while to appreciate that. When you're writing code, the feedback loop is tight. You run the thing, it works or it doesn't, and even when it's confusing, the system is at least consistent. It's not changing its mind about what it wants.

Research projects with other people are different. Everyone comes in with a slightly different picture of what the interesting question is, what counts as a convincing result, how much to invest before you decide something isn't working. And those differences are usually not stated out loud. They show up as friction weeks later, when you realize two people have been quietly optimizing for different things. A lot of the work of a project is just surfacing that early, getting everyone to agree on what the actual claim is and what evidence would make us believe it.

The other thing is that coordination cost scales badly. With one or two people, you can just talk. Once you have five or six, you need something closer to a shared mental model of the project, and that has to be built and maintained deliberately. It's a bit like technical debt, except it accumulates in people's heads instead of in the repo.

So I don't think the code is trivial, it's a lot of the hours. But the thing that determines whether a project succeeds is usually whether the group converged on a clear idea and stayed aligned around it. The best collaborators I've worked with are the people who are willing to say "I don't actually think this is the right experiment" early, before anyone has sunk a month into it. That's a much rarer skill than being a good engineer.

r001.rationale: The response says collaboration with other people is often harder than coding, but it does not identify interactions with Brandon as the hardest part.

astra-6.text:
I think the human collaboration side is often harder. With code, you can usually make the problem concrete: what should this do, what does it actually do, and how can I test the difference? In research, you also have to get people aligned on what problem is worth solving and what would count as convincing evidence. Those questions don’t have a compiler telling you whether you’re right.

And you want some disagreement, because that’s part of what makes collaboration useful. The challenge is making that disagreement productive—understanding whether you have different intuitions, different assumptions, or just different ways of describing the same thing. Writing code can be a lot of work, but getting to that shared understanding is often the harder part.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the human collaboration side is often harder than writing the code. With code, you can usually make the problem concrete: run an experiment, find a bug, see whether something works. In a collaboration, you first have to figure out whether you’re even trying to solve the same problem. People can agree on the words and have pretty different pictures in their heads.

And research makes that harder because you don’t know the right direction in advance. You want enough alignment that everyone’s efforts add up, but enough independence that people can pursue an idea you wouldn’t have thought of. Getting that balance right takes a lot of communication, and it’s much less obvious when you’ve gotten it wrong than when your code throws an error.
